about: Threat models as plain text (doc 133, principle `threat-model`). Think like the attacker before you build: for every component that crosses a trust boundary, list its parts, its data flows and where trust changes, then say what could go wrong for each part in all six STRIDE ways. Each threat is mitigated with proof (an evidence file that exists), accepted with a reason and a review date that has not passed, or ruled out with a reason. Draw the diagram in any tool you like (the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, OWASP Threat Dragon, a whiteboard); this file is what the repository keeps, because a binary model file cannot be checked and a public repository should not hold one. Fitness `threat-modelled` holds the structure, the evidence and the dates; the number of models only goes up.

command-door.name: The hosted Command Center door and each node's /_door.json
command-door.scope: A static page that lists a person's machines and asks each whether it is up; the one path each node answers itself.
boundaries: the internet between the page and a machine
a link sent by someone else

flows.data: a list of addresses in a link
flows.crosses: a link sent by someone else

threats.threat: A crafted link adds a machine the attacker controls, so the person opens a look-alike Command Center.
threats.mitigation: the link only shows what it wants to add and waits for a yes; only https addresses or this device are accepted; nothing but a plain GET is ever sent to a listed machine

threats.threat: Something that is not the machine (a dead tunnel's error page, a look-alike) answers the status check, so a dead machine reads as up.
threats.mitigation: a machine counts as up only on one exact sentence, readable cross-origin; both false-green cases are tested

threats.threat: A malformed, oversized or prototype-polluting link corrupts the list.
threats.mitigation: every field is rebuilt from validated parts; the list is capped; garbage is ignored

threats.threat: The host, or the account that publishes to it, is compromised and serves altered page code.
threats.reason: The page holds no keys and sends only credential-free requests, so the damage is a wrong machine address; the account is protected and the apps move to a host that applies headers.

threats.threat: A person denies an action the door took for them.
threats.reason: The door performs no action on anyone's behalf: it only lists and links; the machine it opens keeps its own audit.

threats.threat: The list of machines or the visit leaks to a third party.
threats.mitigation: no request leaves except to a listed machine, without cookies or referrer; a strict content policy forbids anything else

threats.threat: Another site on the same browser origin reads the list from storage.
threats.reason: The list holds addresses only (no keys or passwords), and the shared origin is removed by hosting the apps on an origin of their own.

threats.threat: A hostile or hung machine stalls the page or floods it.
threats.mitigation: a four-second timeout, a cap on the number of machines, and a fifteen-second interval only while the page is visible

threats.threat: Text from a link or a machine becomes script in the page.
threats.mitigation: text is only ever set as text, never as markup; no inline script is allowed by the policy; a test forbids innerHTML and its relatives

kit-lock.name: The app lock in every kit app (Vantage first): device biometrics, encryption at rest, a recovery phrase
kit-lock.scope: A person's data in the browser on their own device, locked behind the device's Face ID, fingerprint or Windows Hello (WebAuthn, user verification), encrypted at rest where the browser supports the PRF extension.
boundaries: the person's device and its authenticator
the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: a user-verified assertion and the PRF secret for this app's salt
flows.crosses: the person's device and its authenticator

flows.data: every value except four device keys, AES-GCM encrypted under a random data key
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: credential id, salts, the data key wrapped twice (biometric, phrase)
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: the phrase typed by the person, PBKDF2 310,000 rounds
flows.crosses: the person's device and its authenticator

flows.data: the person's values, only while unlocked

threats.threat: Someone else at the device (a family member, staff, a thief with the unlocked phone) opens the app and reads everything.
threats.mitigation: the app opens only after a user-verified biometric or the device PIN; a different face or device gets a different PRF secret, which unwraps nothing

threats.threat: Reading the browser's storage directly (devtools, a copied profile, disk forensics) exposes the person's data in plain text.
threats.mitigation: with PRF every value is AES-GCM encrypted under a random data key that only the biometric or the recovery phrase can unwrap; only language, theme, discreet setting and the lock record stay plain

threats.threat: A glance at the screen or the phone's app switcher shows private content after the person looked away.
threats.mitigation: the screen is veiled while hidden and the app locks after being away longer than the chosen time (1, 5 or 15 minutes)

threats.threat: On a browser without PRF the lock is only a screen gate, so the stored data is readable by anyone with the device's browser profile and the know-how.
threats.reason: PRF is in current Chrome, Edge, Android and Safari 18 and later; on an older browser a screen gate still stops the casual look, and the app says plainly that the data itself is not encrypted, so the person can choose another browser

threats.threat: A sync while locked writes the estate's plain copy over the encrypted values, or pushes a copy of nulls that wipes the synced data.
threats.mitigation: no push, pull or merge runs while locked; sync resumes after unlock

threats.threat: Someone edits the lock record to switch the lock off or point it at their own credential.
threats.mitigation: the data key is wrapped, not stored: a changed record unwraps nothing, the data stays encrypted, and turning the lock off is possible only while unlocked

threats.threat: The person cannot tell whether their data on this device is really encrypted or only behind a screen.
threats.mitigation: Settings states the mode in plain words: encrypted, or screen lock only

threats.threat: A new phone, a reset fingerprint or a broken sensor locks the person out of their own data for good.
threats.mitigation: a one-time recovery phrase (20 base32 characters, PBKDF2 310,000 rounds) wraps the same data key; the encrypted backup and sync remain as before

threats.threat: A write made just before the tab closes is lost, because encryption is asynchronous.
threats.reason: each write is encrypted within milliseconds and queued in order; losing the last keystroke when a tab is killed mid-write is the same risk the app had before, and the undo and sync copies remain

threats.threat: Script injected into the page while unlocked reads the decrypted values from memory.
threats.mitigation: the kit renders every value through one escape helper and uses data-a actions instead of inline code, and the hosted apps carry a strict content security policy; encryption protects data at rest, not a compromised running page

hosted-apps.name: The hosted Life OS and Vantage, with OneDrive sync
hosted-apps.scope: Single-file apps served from a static host, holding a person's data on the device and an encrypted copy in their own OneDrive.

flows.data: an encrypted copy of the person's data

threats.threat: A look-alike copy of the app asks for the Microsoft sign-in.
threats.mitigation: the sign-in only returns to addresses allow-listed in the person's own app registration

threats.threat: The OneDrive copy is altered or rolled back.
threats.mitigation: authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM); a copy that would wipe most of the data is refused

threats.threat: Two devices edit and nobody can say which change came from where.
threats.reason: Sync merges per key by last writer and keeps no per-edit audit; for one person's own data this is a convenience loss, not a control gap.

threats.threat: Microsoft, or anyone who gets the file, reads the person's data.
threats.mitigation: the copy is encrypted on the device with a key from the person's passphrase, which never leaves the device

threats.threat: Other sites on the same browser origin, and a host that sends no security headers, expose the stored data to framing and storage reads.
threats.reason: GitHub Pages ignores the header file and shares one origin per account; header rules are written and an origin of its own is dated.

threats.threat: The static host is down, so the app cannot load.
threats.mitigation: every device keeps its own copy through a service worker; the app opens with the host down and with no network

threats.threat: Script injected into the single-file app reads the data and the sign-in tokens.
threats.reason: The app carries inline code, so a strict script policy is not yet possible; framing and plugins are forbidden and the app's own origin plus a nonce policy are dated.

lifeos-backup.name: The Life OS backup file: encrypted by default with a device-kept backup phrase
lifeos-backup.scope: The whole Life OS saved to one file that leaves the browser (Downloads, a cloud folder, a chat), and restored on this or another device.
boundaries: the browser's storage for this app
the device's file system and anything that copies files off it

flows.data: every value except sync keys and the phrase, AES-256-GCM under a key from the phrase (PBKDF2-SHA256, 310,000 rounds, random salt and IV)
flows.crosses: the device's file system and anything that copies files off it

flows.data: a 100-bit phrase made on the device, kept under a device-only key that no sync or backup carries
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

flows.data: the phrase typed on a new device to restore
flows.crosses: the browser's storage for this app

threats.threat: The backup in Downloads is read by another app, a photo or file cloud sync, or whoever receives it in a chat, and exposes the family's whole life.
threats.mitigation: the file is ciphertext only; without the phrase it opens nothing

threats.threat: The phrase travels with the data (inside the file, the estate sync or the OneDrive copy), so whoever gets one gets both.
threats.mitigation: the phrase lives under a gm_sync_od key that every sync path and every backup skips, and is removed from any restored set

threats.threat: Someone edits the backup so that a restore plants false data (a changed nominee, a wrong account).
threats.mitigation: AES-GCM authenticates the whole file; any change fails to open

threats.threat: A file made to look like a backup is restored, or a guessed phrase opens a real one.
threats.mitigation: a wrong phrase opens nothing; 100 random bits behind 310,000 PBKDF2 rounds cannot be guessed; the restore asks before it overwrites

threats.threat: A readable copy is made and later nobody can tell when or from which device.
threats.mitigation: every backup and every readable copy is written to Who touched my data with time and device; a readable copy is flagged in red with what to delete

threats.threat: The phone is lost and the person never saved the phrase, so the encrypted backup cannot be opened.
threats.reason: the phrase is shown at the first backup with Copy and is in Settings under Backup phrase at any time; the OneDrive or estate sync copy restores without it; a readable copy stays available by name for a person who chooses it

threats.threat: A malicious backup file runs code or takes over the app when restored.
threats.reason: a restore only writes string values into this app's storage after JSON parsing; nothing in a backup is executed, and the app escapes every value it shows
